p.src: Now Lei Heng came to the Hall of the Numinous Officer and saw the burly man asleep upon the offering table. The local soldiers stepped forward, bound him with a rope, and took him away from the hall. By then the sky was already beginning to lighten, for it was the fifth watch. Lei Heng said, “Let us first take this fellow to Headman Chao’s manor, get something to eat, and then escort him to the county offices for questioning.” The whole party accordingly made for the headman’s manor.

p.src: The headman of East Brook Village was surnamed Chao and named Gai. His family had long been wealthy landowners of that county and district. All his life he upheld justice and freely gave away his wealth, and he especially delighted in befriending gallant men from across the realm. Whoever came to seek refuge with him, worthy or otherwise, he allowed to stay at his manor. When they wished to leave, he would also provide them with silver for their journey. He was passionately fond of thrusting with the spear and wielding the staff. Strong and powerfully built himself, he took no wife and spent every day tempering his muscles and bones. Outside the eastern gate in the jurisdiction of Yuncheng County lay two villages, one called East Brook Village and the other West Brook Village, separated only by a broad stream. In former times, ghosts often haunted West Brook Village, bewildering people even in broad daylight and luring them into the water, and nothing could be done about it. Then one day a monk happened to pass through. The villagers told him the whole story, whereupon he pointed out a place and instructed them to carve a pagoda from bluestone and set it there to subdue the evil by the stream. Thereupon all the ghosts of West Brook Village were driven across into East Brook Village. When Chao Gai learned of this, he flew into a rage. He crossed the stream, seized the bluestone pagoda single-handed, carried it back, and set it down in East Brook Village. For this reason everyone called him the “Pagoda-Lifting Heavenly King.” Chao Gai was the unrivalled leading man of that village, and his name was known throughout the world of the rivers and lakes.

p.src: Before long, Lei Heng and the local soldiers brought the prisoner to the manor gate and knocked. When the servants within learned who had come, they reported it to the headman. Chao Gai had not yet risen. Hearing that Patrol Chief Lei had arrived, he hurriedly ordered the gate opened. Once the servants opened the manor gate, the soldiers first suspended the man by his bonds in the gatehouse. Lei Heng himself led a dozen or so of the principal men into the thatched hall, where they sat down. Chao Gai rose to receive them and politely asked, “What official business brings you here, Patrol Chief?” Lei Heng replied, “By the magistrate’s august command, Zhu Tong and I have each led a detachment of local soldiers along separate routes through the villages to patrol for thieves and bandits. We grew weary from walking and wished to rest awhile, so we came directly to your honored manor. I regret disturbing your sleep, Headman.” Chao Gai said, “That is no trouble at all!” He at once ordered the servants to prepare food and wine for his guests and first had hot broth brought for them. Chao Gai then asked, “Did you happen to catch any petty thief in our village?” Lei Heng said, “Just now we found a burly fellow asleep in the Hall of the Numinous Officer. He did not look like an honest gentleman to me. He must have got drunk and simply fallen asleep there. We tied him up with ropes and had intended to take him straight to the county offices to face the magistrate. But first, it was still too early; and second, we wanted you to know of it, so that if the magistrate asks you about it later, you will be prepared to answer. At present he is hanging in your manor’s gatehouse.” Chao Gai heard this and took careful note of it. He thanked Lei Heng, saying, “I am much obliged to you for informing me, Patrol Chief.” Shortly afterward the servants carried out trays of dishes, food, and wine. Chao Gai called out, “This is no fit place for conversation. Let us sit awhile beneath the gallery by the rear hall.” He ordered the servants to light lamps and candles within, then invited the patrol chief inside for a few cups. Chao Gai took the host’s place, and Lei Heng sat in the guest’s seat. When the two were seated, the servants laid out fruit, drinking accompaniments, vegetables, and platters of food. While the servants poured the wine, Chao Gai also ordered wine purchased for all the soldiers. The servants led them to the guest seats beneath the gallery and entertained them there, continually urging them to eat from great platters of meat and drink their fill. As Chao Gai entertained Lei Heng with wine, he privately wondered, “What petty thief from the village could he have caught? I had better go and see for myself who it is.” After keeping him company through five or seven cups, Chao Gai summoned one of his stewards. “Sit with the patrol chief and keep him company. I am going to wash my hands and shall return shortly.”

p.src: The steward remained drinking with Lei Heng, while Chao Gai went inside, took a lantern, and made straight for the gatehouse. When he arrived, all the soldiers had gone off to eat and drink, and not one remained outside. Chao Gai asked the gatekeeper, “Where is the thief caught by the patrol chief being held?” The servant replied, “He is locked in the gatehouse.” Chao Gai pushed open the door and looked inside. He saw the man suspended high within, his whole dark-skinned body exposed. Beneath him, two black and shaggy legs strained against the ropes, and both his feet were bare. Chao Gai shone the lantern upon the man’s face. It was broad and purplish-black, with a vermilion birthmark beside the temple, overgrown with a patch of blackish-yellow hair. Chao Gai asked, “My man, where are you from? I have never seen you in our village before.” The man replied, “I am a traveler from a distant district and came here to seek refuge with someone. Yet they seized me and called me a thief. I shall have a chance to explain myself.” Chao Gai said, “Whom did you come to seek in our village?” The man replied, “I came to this village to seek out a gallant hero.” Chao Gai asked, “What is this hero’s name?” The man replied, “He is called Headman Chao.” Chao Gai said, “And what business do you have with him?” The man replied, “He is a righteous and gallant man renowned throughout the realm. p.src: Before he had finished speaking, the man cried out, “Uncle, save me!” Chao Gai pretended to look him over, then demanded, “Why, isn’t this fellow Wang Xiaosan?” The man said, “That is who I am. Uncle, save me.” Everyone was startled. Lei Heng asked Chao Gai, “Who is this man? How does he come to know you, Headman?” Chao Gai said, “It turns out he is my nephew, Wang Xiaosan. What was the fellow doing sleeping in the temple? He is my elder sister’s boy. He was raised here from childhood, but when he was four or five he went with my sister and her husband to live in the Southern Capital, and remained away for more than ten years. When he was fourteen or fifteen he came back once, accompanying a merchant from the capital who came here to trade, but I have not seen him since. I have often heard that he has turned out badly. How has he come to be here? I myself could scarcely recognize him, but there is a patch of vermilion birthmark beside his temple, and by that I knew him vaguely.” Chao Gai shouted, “Xiaosan, why did you not come straight to see me? Why did you go thieving in the village instead?” The man cried, “Uncle, I committed no theft.” Chao Gai roared, “If you did not steal, why were you seized and brought here?” He snatched a staff from a militiaman’s hand and struck at the man’s head and face. Lei Heng and the others restrained him, saying, “Do not beat him yet. Hear what he has to say.” The man said, “Uncle, calm your anger and hear me out. Is it not ten years now since I last came here at fourteen or fifteen? Last night I drank a cup too many on the road and dared not come to see you, so I went to sleep it off in the temple, intending to seek you once I was sober; but unexpectedly they seized me without asking why I was there. I have committed no theft.” Chao Gai raised the staff to strike him again and cursed, “You brute! Instead of coming straight to see me, you stopped on the road to swill that yellow liquor! Was there no wine in my house for you to drink? You have disgraced me utterly!” Lei Heng urged him, “Calm yourself, Headman. Your nephew truly committed no theft. We found such a great strapping stranger sleeping suspiciously in the temple; his face was unfamiliar and none of us knew him, so we became suspicious and brought him here under arrest. Had we known sooner that he was your nephew, we certainly would not have seized him.” He ordered the militiamen to untie the ropes at once and hand the man over to the headman. The militiamen immediately released the man. Lei Heng said, “Please do not take offense, Headman. Had we known he was your nephew, matters would never have come to this. We have gravely offended you. We shall take our leave.” Chao Gai said, “Stay a while, Constable. Please come into my humble manor; there is more I would say.”

We could devise a sound plan to seize it on the road. Heaven itself would approve, and it would be no crime. I have heard of your great name, Brother: that you are a true man and surpassingly skilled in arms. Though I have little talent, I too have learned some skill. Let alone three or five men—even amid a force of one or two thousand soldiers and horsemen, I would fear no one with a spear in my hands. But I cannot stomach that scoundrel Lei Heng cheating Headman Chao out of ten taels of silver for nothing, after stringing me up all night.
They cannot have gone far. I had better take a staff and overtake them, knock the whole band down, recover the silver, and return it to Chao Gai. That will also vent my anger.
An excellent plan!”
Liu Tang left the room, took a broad-bladed sword from the weapon rack, went out through the manor gate, and strode southward in pursuit.
By then the sky was already brightening. Behold:

p.src: The Northern Dipper had just turned crosswise; the eastern sky was paling. At the world’s farthest edge, the first light of dawn had barely spread; above the sea’s remotest corner, the last stars slowly sank. Thrice the golden cock crowed, calling fair ladies to powder their faces and apply rouge; Fine steeds neighed again and again, urging travelers onward in their rivalry for fame and profit. A few strands of crimson cloud stretched across the azure heavens, and a round red sun rose over Fusang.

p.src: Lei Heng started in alarm and turned to see Liu Tang racing after him, a broad-bladed sword in hand. Lei Heng hurriedly snatched a broad-bladed sword from one of his soldiers and shouted, “What are you chasing me for, you rogue?” Liu Tang said, “If you know what is good for you, leave those ten taels of silver and give them back to me. Then I’ll spare you!” Lei Heng said, “Your uncle gave them to me. What business is it of yours? Were it not for your uncle’s sake, I would have finished you off on the spot. Yet you have the gall to demand the silver from me?” Liu Tang said, “I’m no bandit, yet you strung me up for a whole night and then swindled ten taels of silver out of my uncle. If you have any sense, bring it back to me, and I’ll treat you with all courtesy; but if you refuse, I’ll make you spill blood here and now!” Lei Heng flew into a rage, pointed at Liu Tang, and cursed him: “You lying thief who disgraces his house and ruins his family! How dare you behave so insolently!” Liu Tang said, “You filthy scoundrel who extorts and victimizes the common folk! How dare you curse me!” Lei Heng cursed him again: “With that thieving head, thieving face, and thieving carcass of yours, you are certain to bring trouble upon Chao Gai! A man with such a thief’s heart and guts cannot travel under my jurisdiction!” Liu Tang raged, “Then let you and me settle which of us is the better man.” Brandishing his broad-bladed sword, he charged straight at Lei Heng. Seeing Liu Tang rush upon him, Lei Heng laughed aloud and thrust out his own broad-bladed sword to meet him. The two clashed there on the highway. Behold:

p.src: Back and forth they moved, like phoenixes turning in flight; They lunged and charged, like eagles spreading their wings. One thrust straight at his mark, every stroke true to the finest method; The other parried and barred, displaying an understanding all his own. This one, with a T-shaped step, pressed swiftly in; That one, with a four-change turn, drove forward. As the couplet says: Though they shall never ascend the Pavilion of Soaring Mist, this scene itself deserves a painted scroll.

p.src: Lei Heng and Liu Tang fought more than fifty bouts there on the road, with neither gaining the upper hand. When the soldiers saw that Lei Heng could not overcome Liu Tang, they prepared to fall upon him all together. Just then a wicket in a fence to one side opened, and a man emerged flourishing two bronze chains. “You two good fellows, stop fighting!” he called. “I have been watching for some time. Rest awhile—I have something to say.” He thrust the bronze chains between them. Both men checked their swords, leapt out of the fighting circle, and stood their ground. The newcomer was dressed like a scholar. He wore a cylindrical headscarf low over his brows, a loose hempen gown edged in black, and a tawny-brown ornamental sash about his waist; below, he wore silk shoes and spotless socks. His brows were fine, his eyes handsome, his face pale, and his beard long. This man was Wu Yong, known as the “Resourceful Star.” His courtesy name was Pedagogue, his Taoist name was Master Illuminating, and his family had long belonged to that very district. There was once a lyric to the tune “Immortal by the River” extolling Wu Yong’s gifts: He had read ten thousand volumes of the classics; all his life his nimble mind had teemed with ingenious devices, and he had mastered the Six Secret Teachings and the Three Strategies. Within his breast were warrior generals concealed; within his belly, mighty hosts lay hidden. In strategy he dared surpass Zhuge Liang; how could Chen Ping rival his talents? The slightest scheme from him would startle ghosts and gods. By courtesy name he was called Pedagogue Wu; by sobriquet, the “Resourceful Star.”

p.src: Wu Yong stood holding his bronze chains and called to Liu Tang, “Hold there, fellow! Why are you quarrelling with the chief constable?” Liu Tang glared at Wu Yong and said, “This is none of your business, scholar!” Lei Heng said, “You do not know the story, Teacher. Last night this rogue was sleeping stark naked in the Temple of the Divine Marshal. We seized him and took him to Village Head Chao’s manor. He turned out to be the village head’s nephew, so for his uncle’s sake I released him. Heavenly King Chao treated us to wine and gave me a few gifts. But this rogue hid it from his uncle and chased me all the way here to demand them back. Would you not call that brazen?” Wu Yong thought, “Chao Gai and I have been friends since childhood. Whenever anything arises, he discusses his plans with me. I know all his relatives and acquaintances, but I have never seen this nephew. Besides, their ages do not fit the relationship. There must be something strange here. First I had better stop this commotion; afterward I can question him.” Wu Yong then said, “Good fellow, do not persist in your folly. Your uncle is a close friend of mine and is also on good terms with this chief constable. If he gave the constable a token of friendship and you now demand it back, you will surely cause your uncle to lose face. For my sake, let the matter rest. I shall speak to your uncle myself.” Liu Tang said, “Scholar, you do not understand. My uncle did not willingly give him that silver. He swindled it out of him; and if he does not return it, I swear I will not go back.” Lei Heng said, “I’ll return it only if the village head comes to claim it himself. I will not give it to you.” Liu Tang said, “You falsely accused an innocent man of being a thief and swindled away the silver. Why should you not return it?” Lei Heng said, “It is not your silver. I won’t return it—I won’t!” Liu Tang said, “So you refuse to return it! Then ask the broad-bladed sword in my hand whether it will let the matter rest.” Wu Yong tried again to dissuade them: “You two have fought for half the day without either winning. How long do you mean to keep it up?” Liu Tang said, “If he will not return my silver, I’ll fight him until one of us is dead.” Lei Heng raged, “If I were afraid of you, I could add even one soldier to the fight and still not deserve to be called a true man. Come what may, I shall run you through myself, and that will settle it!” Liu Tang flew into a rage, beat his chest, and cried, “I am not afraid! Not afraid!” Then he rushed forward. Lei Heng, gesticulating furiously, advanced from the other side. The two were about to clash again. Wu Yong placed himself crosswise between them and pleaded, but there was no restraining them. Liu Tang gripped his broad-bladed sword and was about to force his way past. Lei Heng poured forth an endless torrent of abuse about thieves, raised his broad-bladed sword, and stood ready to fight. Just then the soldiers pointed and cried, “The village head is coming!”

p.src: Liu Tang turned and saw Chao Gai hurrying along the highway, a robe thrown over his shoulders and its front hanging open. “You brute, cease your insolence!” Chao Gai thundered. Wu Yong laughed aloud. “Only when the village head comes himself can this quarrel finally be stopped.” Chao Gai arrived panting and asked, “Why did you chase him here and start fighting with broad-bladed swords?” Lei Heng said, “Your worthy nephew came after me with a broad-bladed sword and demanded the silver back. I told him, ‘I will not return it to you. I shall personally return it to the village head, and the matter is none of your concern.’ He fought fifty bouts with me, and the Teacher has been here trying to make peace.” Chao Gai said, “The brute! I knew nothing of this. Chief Constable, please return for my sake. I shall call at your door another day to apologize.” Lei Heng said, “I know the rogue was acting recklessly, so I will not lower myself to his level. I am sorry to have made you come so far, Village Head.” He took his leave and went away; there is no more to tell of it.

p.src: Now Wu Yong said to Chao Gai, “Had you not come yourself, Headman, a grave affair would nearly have occurred. This nephew of yours is truly extraordinary and possesses excellent martial skill. I watched them from behind the fence. Even Constable Lei, renowned for his mastery of the broad-bladed sword, could not prevail against him and could do no more than parry and defend. Had they fought a few more bouts, Lei Heng would certainly have lost his life, so I hurried out to separate them. Where did this nephew of yours come from? I have never seen him at your manor before.” Chao Gai replied, “I was just about to invite you to my humble manor to discuss something. I meant to send someone for you, but then I found he had disappeared, and the broad-bladed sword was missing from its rack as well. Then a herd boy reported that a burly fellow carrying a broad-bladed sword had gone racing straight south. I hurried after him, and fortunately you, Master, had already remonstrated with him and stopped him. Please honor my humble manor with your presence; there is a matter I should like to discuss with you.” Wu Yong returned to the schoolroom, hung the bronze chain inside, and instructed the master of the house, “When the pupils come, tell them that their teacher has business today and is granting them a day’s leave.” A poem bears witness: His literary gifts were no less lofty than his martial skill; even a bronze chain could restrain a broad-bladed sword. He loved lofty talk in the company of righteous men; how could he willingly sit idly among mere children? Release all those birds from their cage, and let the clamorous frogs leap in the fields. The teacher was ever fond of action; the pupils rejoiced, while their parents fretted.

p.src: Wu Yong pulled the schoolroom door shut and locked it, then went with Chao Gai and Liu Tang to Chao Family Manor. Chao Gai led them directly into a secluded rear hall, where host and guests took their respective seats. Wu Yong asked, “Headman, who is this man?” Chao Gai replied, “He is a gallant of the rivers and lakes. His surname is Liu, his given name Tang, and he comes from East Luzhou. He learned of a rich prize and came especially to seek my aid. Last night he lay drunk in the Temple of the Divine Officer, where Lei Heng arrested him and brought him to my manor. Only after I claimed him as my nephew was he able to get free. He said, ‘Liang Zhongshu of the Daming Prefecture in the Northern Capital has purchased gold, pearls, and precious objects worth a hundred thousand strings of cash. He is sending them to the Eastern Capital as a birthday gift for his father-in-law, Grand Preceptor Cai, and they will pass this way before long. What harm is there in taking such ill-gotten wealth?’ His arrival corresponds exactly to a dream I had. Last night I dreamed that the seven stars of the Northern Dipper fell straight onto the ridge of my house, while another small star beside the Dipper’s handle turned into a streak of white light and vanished. I thought: if the stars shine upon my house, how could this fail to bring good fortune? This very morning I intended to invite you, Master, to discuss what should be done about this affair.” Wu Yong smiled. “When I saw Brother Liu come racing after us in such strange circumstances, I had already guessed seventy or eighty percent of the matter. The scheme is a fine one, but there is one difficulty: it cannot be accomplished by too many men, nor can it be accomplished by too few. Though your manor is full of retainers, not one of them can be used. At present there are only you, Brother Liu, and myself. How can the three of us manage this affair? Even though you and Brother Liu are exceptionally capable, the burden is still too great for you to bear. This undertaking requires seven or eight true gallants; any more would be useless.” Chao Gai said, “Could that number be meant to correspond to the stars in my dream?” Wu Yong replied at once, “Your dream is no ordinary matter, elder brother. Could it mean that more men are coming from the north to aid us?” Wu Yong pondered for a long while. Then his brows lifted as a plan came to him, and he cried, “I have it! I have it!” Chao Gai said, “If you know trustworthy gallants, Master, we should invite them here at once and bring this undertaking to fruition.”
